newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Eurobourses close strongly, lifted by Clinton.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Eurobourses close strongly, lifted by Clinton.

text.p: European bourses registered strong gains on Wednesday as investors saw the U.S. electorate's decision not to rock the boat as good for business.

On currency markets, the dollar strengthened rapidly on the news of President Clinton's re-election and the Republicans retaining their grip on Congress, but profit-takers moved in and took some of the shine off the currency.

Frankfurt and Paris ended trade well over one percent up, cheered by the Republican victory in the House and Senate, which was seen as promising stable economic policies. And, as if on schedule, Wall Street jumped nearly one percent in early trade.

Investors on both sides of the Atlantic turned bullish amid hopes that the lid would stay on U.S. government spending after worries that big Democrat inroads in Congress would mean increased public spending.
"The mark-up was on the cards after we got what looks like the ideal outcome to the U.S. election," one dealer said.
In Paris, stocks ended at a high for the year after investors had gone on a big 7.3 billion franc ($1.4 billion) buying spree in approval of the election result.
"It's an exceptional volume," said one trader. "This is not a rise in a vacuum." The blue-chip CAC-40 index closed up 26.05 points or 1.19 percent at 2,213.37.

The best performer was Frankfurt where floor trading registered a gain of 1.4 percent, helped by the Clinton win, overnight gains on Wall Street and the firmer dollar. London put on the poorest showing, with the FTSE index ending only 0.4 percent higher. Election optimism was eroded by fears over more interest rate hikes after last week's surprise rise of 0.25 percentage point.
The Bank of England warned Britain's Conservative government it was unlikely to meet its 2.5 percent inflation target and would probably have to raise interest rates again.
In its quarterly Inflation Report, the central bank welcomed finance minister Kenneth Clarke's move raising interest rates but made it clear he could not rest on his laurels.
"There is now much less chance of inflation being below 2-1/2 percent during 1997. Achievement of the inflation target remains elusive," it said.
In Madrid, stocks rose to historic peaks at one point, sharing the euphoria in Europe but later slipped back. Spanish bonds also hit new highs.

Wall Street itself jumped more than 50 points in early trading to 6,135 points. High tech stocks were up sharply, because of the defeat of Proposition 211 in California which would have made it easier for shareholders to sue companies.
The dollar shed some of its early gains on the mark and yen. By late European trading it had slipped to Tuesday's closing levels on profit-taking.
"We have seen profit-taking across the board, especially on dollar/mark and dollar/yen," said a trader at a U.S. bank.
The foreign exchanges were cheered in early transactions by Clinton's win but were clearly relieved his hands will be tied by a Republican Congress, regarded as pro-business.
Analysts said the dollar's prospects looked healthy.

"Markets believe Clinton will keep a tight rein on the Republican tax cutting agenda, while the Republican Congress will operate to keep his spending priorities in check," Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank said.
CURRENCIES
The dollar was at 1.5185 marks and 113.97 yen in late European trading, compared with 1.5188 and 114.05 on Tuesday.
STOCK MARKETS - CLOSING INDICES
The Financial Times-Stock Exchange index of 100 leading British shares ended 14.6 points higher at 3,935.7.
In Paris, the CAC-40 share index finished up 26.05 at 2,213.37.
The 30-share DAX index in Frankfurt closed up 37.90 at 2,729.19.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold closed at $378.15, compared with $379.35 at the close on Tuesday. Silver was six cents down at $4.78.
